analysis.title: Technology volatility, the AI cycle, and what's next for investors
key_insights: US midterm elections in early November 2026 produced a backlash against data centre development. Stricter licensing and possible removal of tax breaks in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, which hold a large share of AI data-centre buildout, could raise hyperscaler costs and reduce returns on investment.

Technology stocks sold off sharply after the midterms. Fidelity's view is that AI's long-term growth story is intact and that political scrutiny and regulation may slow, not stop, US data centre development.

Fidelity's Matt Quaife attributes the sell-off mainly to technical selling from passive and systematic strategies. Retail investors, some using leverage, had driven the semiconductor and tech hardware rally in the first three quarters of 2026 and were forced to liquidate as the market turned, amplifying the weakness.

Fidelity equity analyst Austin Kelly sees indiscriminate selling: several tech companies have strong structural AI-driven growth, very high returns on capital and reasonable valuation multiples. He expects the fear to prove worse than the eventual reality.

Fidelity's Salman Ahmed argues both parties are incentivised to keep AI investment going. AI investment has been a major driver of US GDP growth in recent quarters, and the US economy would be close to recession without it. Allowing China an AI lead is unacceptable to both parties, so further buildout is likely to proceed with possible added regulation or oversight.

Forward P/E ratios for the Nasdaq and MSCI AC World are below their historic averages, reflecting strong 2027+ earnings growth forecasts. IT sector 2027 earnings are forecast around 150% above the 2022-2026 average, and MSCI AC World consensus earnings growth is above 50%.

The key question for tech and other sectors is whether those earnings expectations are realistic and how resilient earnings are to a tougher political backdrop. Fidelity's research teams are watching for signs that exceptionally strong growth rates are eroding.

Multi Asset positioning: Quaife's team has added risk cautiously in recent days. In fixed income they prefer short-duration credit over sovereign debt, expect no meaningful GDP deterioration, and say geopolitical and inflation risks make sovereign bond return forecasts too uncertain.
Delays to the AI build-out matter for infrastructure firms and utilities. AI adoption is also replacing legacy systems at banks and insurers, with implications for productivity and margins.
Fidelity stresses diversification and position sizing because correlations remain high across regions and sectors, and recommends re-testing assumptions and adjusting when ideas prove wrong.

sector_views.rationale: Long-term AI growth intact and selected names attractively valued after indiscriminate selling, but the multi-asset team is adding risk only cautiously given political and positioning risk.
Potential delays to the AI build-out are an important variable for these sectors.
AI tools are replacing legacy systems at banks and insurers, with implications for productivity and margins.
